body.translated_text: As for the statement that has been cited as contradicting perception—"This one, armed with sacrificial implements (<s>yajñāyudhī</s>), the sacrificer, goes directly to the heavenly world"—which designates the perceptible body, to that it is replied: due to the connection with the body, the one whose body that is, he too is called <s>yajñāyudhī</s> (armed with sacrificial implements) by virtue of those sacrificial implements.

body.text: āha : ko ' sāv anyo ? nainam upalabhāmahe / - nanu prāṇādibhir enam upalabhāmahe / yo 'sau prāṇiti apāniti ucchvasiti nimiṣati ityādi ceṣṭitavān, so 'tra śarīre yajñāyudhīti / - nanu śarīram eva prāṇity apāniti ca ? - na prāṇādayaḥ śarīraguṇāḥ / śarīraguṇavidharmāṇo hi te, ayāvaccharīrabhāvitvāt / yāvaccharīraṃ tāvad asya guṇā rūpādayaḥ / prāṇādayas tu saty api śarīre na bhavanti / ato na śarīraguṇāḥ prāṇādayaḥ / sukhādayaś ca svayam upalabhyante, na rūpādaya iva śarīraguṇāḥ pareṇāpi / tasmāc charīraguṇavaidharmyād anyaḥ śarīrād yajñāyudhīti /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] Who is this other [entity]? We do not perceive it. — [Reply:] But we do perceive it through <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath) and the like. The one who breathes in, breathes out, exhales, blinks, and performs such activities—he is the one in this body who is called <s>yajñāyudhī</s>. — [Objection:] But is it not the body itself that breathes in and breathes out? — [Reply:] No, <s>prāṇa</s> and the like are not qualities of the body. For they are dissimilar to the qualities of the body, since they do not persist as long as the body persists. As long as the body exists, its qualities such as <s>rūpa</s> (form) and the like persist. But <s>prāṇa</s> and the like do not exist even when the body exists [i.e., in a corpse]. Therefore <s>prāṇa</s> and the like are not qualities of the body. Moreover, <s>sukha</s> (pleasure) and the like are perceived by oneself, not by another as are body-qualities like form. Therefore, due to the dissimilarity from body-qualities, the one armed with sacrificial implements is other than the body.

body.text: āha : kuta eṣa saṃpratyayaḥ śukhādibhyo 'nyas tadvān asti" iti ? na hi sukhādipratyākhyānena tasya svarūpam upalabhāmahe / tasmāc chaśaviśāṇavad asau nāsti / - athocyate: tena vinā kasya sukhādaya iti ?
body.translated_text: [Objection:] Whence comes this conviction that "there exists a possessor of pleasure and the like who is other than pleasure etc."? For we do not perceive its essential nature by setting aside pleasure and the like. Therefore, like the horn of a hare, it does not exist. — [Reply:] It is said: without that [self], whose are these pleasures and the like?

body.text: - na kasyacid api iti vakyāmaḥ / na hi yo ya upalabhyate, tasya tasya saṃbandhinā bhavitavyam / yasya saṃbandho 'py upalabhyate saṃbandhī ca, tasya ayaṃ saṃbandhīti gamyate / na hi candramasam ādityaṃ vā upalabhya saṃbandhyantarānveoaṇā bhavati "kasyāyam" iti / na kasyacid api ity avadhāryate / tasmān na sukhādibhyo 'nyas tadvān astīti / athopalabdhasya avaśyaṃ kalpayitavyaḥ saṃbandhī bhavet / - tata ātmānam apy anena prakāreṇa upalabhya "kasyāyam" iti saṃbandhyantaram anviṣyema / tam api kalpayitvā 'nyam api kalpayitvā 'nyam ity anavasthaiva syāt / atha kaṃcit kalpayitvā na saṃbandhyantaram api kalpayiṣyasi tāvaty eva viraṃsyasi tāvatā ca paritokṣyasi, tato vijñāna eva parituṣya tāvaty eva virantum arhasi /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] We shall say they belong to no one at all. For it is not the case that for everything perceived, a correlate must necessarily exist. When both a relation and a correlate are perceived, one understands "this is its correlate." For upon perceiving the moon or the sun, there is no search for another correlate asking "to whom does this belong?" It is simply determined that it belongs to no one at all. Therefore there is no possessor of pleasure and the like other than them. And if for every perceived thing a correlate must necessarily be postulated, then having perceived the <s>ātman</s> (self) in this manner, we would also have to search for another correlate—"to whom does this belong?" And having postulated that, then postulating yet another, and another—there would be an infinite regress (<s>anavasthā</s>). If, however, having postulated something, you will not postulate a further correlate but will stop there and be satisfied with that much, then you should be satisfied with <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness) alone and stop right there.

body.text: atrocyate: yadi vijñānād anyo vijñātā nāsti, kas tarhi "jānāti" ity ucyate ? jñānasya kartur abhidhānam anena śabdenopapadyate / tad eṣa śabdo 'rthavān kartavya iti jñānād vyatiriktam ātmānaṃ kalpayiṣyāma iti /
body.translated_text: To this it is replied: if there is no knower other than <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness), then who is referred to when one says "he knows"? The designation of an agent of knowledge is warranted by this word. Therefore, in order to make this word meaningful, we shall postulate an <s>ātman</s> (self) distinct from knowledge.

body.text: āha : devā enaṃ śabdam arthavantaṃ kalpayiṣyanti, yadi kalpayitavyaṃ maṃsyante / bahavaḥ khalv iha janā "asty ātmā, asty ātmā" ity ātmasattāvādina eva śabdasya pratyakṣavaktāro bhavanti, tathāpi nātmasattāṃ kalpayituṃ ghaṭante, kim aṅga punar "jānāti" iti parokṣaśabdadarśanāt / tasmād asad etat /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] The gods will make this word meaningful, if they consider it needs to be made meaningful. Indeed, many people here who explicitly declare "the <s>ātman</s> exists, the <s>ātman</s> exists" are direct proponents of the existence of the self through words, yet even so they are unable to establish the existence of the self; how much less, then, from the observation of an indirect word like "he knows"! Therefore this [argument] is invalid.

body.text: ucyate: icchayā ātmānam upalabhāmahe / - katham ? - upalabdhapūrve hy abhiprete bhavati icchā, nānupalabdhapūrve / yathā merum uttareṇa yāny asmajjātīyair anupalabdhapūrvāṇi svādūni vṛkṣaphalāni, na tānipraty asmākam icchā bhavati / no khalv anyena puruṣeṇa upalabdhe 'pi viṣaye 'nyasyānupalabdhur icchā bhavati / bhavati cānyedyur upalabdhe 'paredyur icchā / atas tenopalambhanena samānakartṛkā sā ityavagacchāmaḥ / yadi vijñānamātram evedam upalambhakam abhaviṣyat, pradhvaste tasmin kasyāparedyur icchā 'bhaviṣyat / atha vijñānād anyo vijñātā nityas, tata ekasmin ahani ya upalabdhā, aparedyur api sa evaiṣiṣyati / itarathā icchānupapannā syāt /
body.translated_text: [Reply:] It is said: we perceive the <s>ātman</s> (self) through desire (<s>icchā</s>). — How? — For desire arises only toward something previously perceived that is desired, not toward something not previously perceived. Just as we have no desire for the sweet tree-fruits beyond <s>Meru</s> to the north, which have never been perceived by people of our kind. Indeed, even when an object has been perceived by another person, desire does not arise in one who has not himself perceived it. But desire on a later day does arise for something perceived on an earlier day. From this we understand that desire has the same agent as that prior perception. If <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness) alone were the perceiver, then when it has perished, whose desire would arise on the following day? But if the knower is permanent and different from consciousness, then the one who perceived on one day will also desire on the following day. Otherwise, desire would be inexplicable.

body.text: atrāha : anupapannam iti naḥ kva saṃpratyayaḥ ? yan na pramāṇena avagatam / vijñānāt tāvad anyan nopalabhāmahe / yac ca nopalabhāmahe, tac chaśaviṣāṇavad eva nāsti ity avagacchāmaḥ / na ca tasmin asati vijñānasadbhāvo 'nupapannaḥ, pratyakṣāvagatatvād eva / kṣaṇikatvaṃ cāsya pratyakṣapūrvakam eva / na ca jñātari vijñānād anyasmin asati jñāne cānitye aparedyur icchā anupapannā, pratyakṣāvagatatvād eva / no khalv apy etad dṛṣṭaṃ "ya evānyedyur upalabhā, sa evāparedyur eṣitā" iti / idaṃ tu dṛṣṭaṃ yat "kvacid anyena dṛṣṭam anya icchati, kvacin na ; samānāyāṃ santatāv anya icchati, santatyantare necchati" iti / tasmān na sukhādivyatirikto 'nyo 'stīti /
body.translated_text: [The Buddhist] objects here: Where is our confidence that [something is] "impossible"? That which is not known through a valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) [need not exist]. We do not apprehend anything other than consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>). And what we do not apprehend, we understand to not exist — like the horn of a hare. Nor is the existence of consciousness impossible even without that [permanent self], since it is known through direct perception alone. Its momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>) too is based on perception alone. And even when there is no knower other than consciousness and when cognition is impermanent, desire on a subsequent day is not impossible — since it is known through direct perception alone. Indeed, it is not observed that "the very one who perceived on a previous day is the one who desires on a subsequent day." But this is observed: "Sometimes what one person sees, another desires, and sometimes not; within the same continuum (<s>santati</s>), one desires, but across a different continuum, one does not." Therefore, there is nothing that exists apart from pleasure (<s>sukha</s>) and the like [i.e., the aggregates].

body.text: atrocyate: na hy "asmartāra icchanti" ity upapadyate / na cādṛṣṭapūrve smṛtir bhavati / tasmāt kṣaṇike vijñānaskandhamātre smṛtir anupapanneti /
body.translated_text: To this it is replied: It is not tenable that "those who do not remember [still] desire." Nor does memory (<s>smṛti</s>) arise regarding what was not previously seen. Therefore, memory is impossible in what is merely a momentary aggregate of consciousness (<s>vijñāna-skandha</s>).

body.text: atrāha : smṛtir api icchāvat / pūrvavijñānasadṛśaṃ vijñānaṃ pūrvavijñānaviṣayaṃ vā smṛtir ity ucyate / tac ca draṣṭari vinaṣṭe 'py aparedyur utpadyamānaṃ nānupapannam, pratyakṣāvagatatvād eva / anyasmin skandhaghane 'nyena skandhaghanena yaj jñānaṃ, tat tatsantatijena anyenopalabhyate nātatsantatijena / tasmāc chūnyāḥ skandhaghanā iti / athāsmin arthe brāhmaṇam bhavati: "vijñānaghana evaitebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ samutthāya tāny eva anuvinaśyati: na pretya saṃjñāsti" iti /
body.translated_text: [The Buddhist] objects here: Memory too is like desire. A cognition similar to a previous cognition, or a cognition having a previous cognition as its object — that is called memory (<s>smṛti</s>). And its arising on a subsequent day, even when the seer has perished, is not impossible — since it is known through direct perception alone. The knowledge that arises in one aggregate-mass (<s>skandha-ghana</s>) from another aggregate-mass is apprehended by another [cognition] belonging to the same continuum, not by one not belonging to that continuum. Therefore, the aggregate-masses are empty [of self]. Moreover, there is a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> text in this regard: "Having arisen as a mass of consciousness (<s>vijñāna-ghana</s>) from these elements, it perishes along with them — there is no awareness after death."

body.text:
atrocyate: naitad evam / anyedyur dṛṣṭe 'paredyur "aham idam adarśam" iti bhavati pratyayaḥ / pratyagātmani caitad bhavati, na paratra / paro hy asau yo 'nyedyur dṛṣṭavān / tasmāt tadvyatirikto 'nyo 'sti, yatrāyam ahaṃśabdaḥ /
āha : paratrāpy ahaṃśabdo bhaktyā dṛśyate, tad yathā "aham eva putro, 'ham eva devadatto, 'ham eva gacchāmi" iti /
body.translated_text: To this it is replied: This is not so. When something was seen on a previous day, on the subsequent day there arises the cognition "I saw this." And this occurs with respect to one's own inner self (<s>pratyagātman</s>), not with respect to another. For the one who saw on the previous day would [otherwise] be another person. Therefore, there exists something distinct from that [consciousness], to which this word "I" (<s>aham</s>) refers. — [The Buddhist] says: The word "I" is seen to be used figuratively (<s>bhaktyā</s>) even with respect to another, as in "I am the son, I am <s>Devadatta</s>, I am going."

body.text: atrocyate: na vayam "aham" itīmaṃ śabdaṃ prayujyamānam anyasmin arthe hetutvena vyapadiśāmaḥ, kiṃ tarhi śabdād vyatiriktaṃ pratyabhijñāpratyayam / pratīmo hi vayam imam arthaṃ "vayam evānyedyur upalabhāmahe, vayam evādya smarāma" iti / tasmād vayam imam artham avagacchāmo "vayam eva hyo, vayam evādya" itil / ye cāmī hyo 'dya ca, na te vinaṣṭāḥ / athāpy asmin arthe brāhmaṇaṃ bhavati / śa vāre 'yam ātmā" iti prakṛtya āmananti "aśīryo na hi śīryata" iti / tathā "avināśī vāre 'yam ātmā anucchittidharmā" iti / vinaśvaraṃ ca vijñānam / tasmād vinaśvarād anyaḥ sa ity avagacchāmaḥ / na ca śakyam evam avagantuṃ "yathopalabhyante 'rthā na tathā bhavanti, yathā tu khalu nopalabhyante tathā bhavanti" iti / tathā hi sati "śaśo nāsti, śaśasya viṣāṇam asti" ity avagamyeta / na ca ahampratyayo vyāmoha iti śakyate vaktum, bādhakapratyayābhāvāt / tasmāt sukhādibhyo vyatirikto 'sti / evaṃ cet, sa eva yajñāyudhī iti vyapadiśyate /
body.translated_text: To this it is replied: We do not cite this word "I" being employed with respect to another object as our proof; rather, [we cite] the recognition-cognition (<s>pratyabhijñā-pratyaya</s>) that is distinct from the word. For we cognize this fact: "We ourselves perceived on the previous day, we ourselves remember today." Therefore, we understand: "We are the same as yesterday, we are the same today." And those who [existed] yesterday and today have not perished. Moreover, there is a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> text in this regard. Beginning with "This self (<s>ātman</s>) indeed..." they teach: "It is without decay, for it does not decay." Likewise: "This self is indeed imperishable, having the nature of non-destruction." But consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) is perishable. Therefore, we understand that it [the self] is different from the perishable [consciousness]. Nor can one maintain that "things are not as they are perceived, but rather they are as they are not perceived" — for then one would have to accept that "the hare does not exist, [but] the hare's horn exists." Nor can the I-cognition (<s>aham-pratyaya</s>) be said to be a delusion, because there is no overriding cognition to contradict it. Therefore, [the self] exists as distinct from pleasure and the like [the aggregates]. And if so, it is that very [self] that is designated as "armed with sacrificial implements" (<s>yajñāyudhī</s>).

body.text: āha : yadi vijñānād anyad asti vijñātṛ, vijñānam apāsya tan nidarśyatām "idaṃ tad īdṛśaṃ ca" iti / na ca tan nidarśyate / tasmān na tato 'nyad asti iti /
body.translated_text: [The Buddhist] says: If there exists a knower distinct from consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>), then setting aside consciousness, show that [knower], saying "this is it, and it is of such-and-such a nature." But that cannot be shown. Therefore, nothing other than that [consciousness] exists.

body.text:
atrocyate: svasaṃvedyaḥ sa bhavati / nāsāv anyena śakyate draṣṭum / katham asau nidarśyeteti ? yathā ca kaścic cakṣuṣmān svayaṃ rūpaṃ paśyati na ca śaknoty anyasmai jātyandhāya tan nidarśayituṃ, na ca "tan na śakyate nidarśayitum" ity etāvatā ṅāsti" ity avagamyate, evam asau puruṣaḥ svayam ātmānam upalabhate na cānyasmai śaknoti darśayitum, anyasya draṣṭus taṃ puruṣaṃ prati darśanaśaktyabhāvāt / so 'py anyaḥ puruṣaḥ svayam ātmānam upalabhate, na parātmānam / tena sarve svena svenātmanā ātmānam upalabhamānāḥ santy eva, yady api parapuruṣair nopalabhyanta iti / athāsmin arthe brāhmaṇaṃ bhavati "śāntāyāṃ vāci kiṃjyotir evāyaṃ puruṣaḥ ? ātmajyotiḥ, samrāḍ iti hovāca" iti / pareṇa nopalabhyata ity atrāpi brāhmaṇaṃ bhavati "agṛhyo na hi gṛhyata" iti / pareṇa na gṛhyata ity etadabhiprāyam etat / - kutaḥ?svayaṃjyotiṣṭvavacanāt / atrāpi brāhmaṇaṃ bhavati "atrāyaṃ puruṣaḥ
svayaṃjyotir bhavati" iti /
body.translated_text: To this it is replied: It [the self] is self-known (<s>svasaṃvedya</s>). It cannot be perceived by another. How then can it be demonstrated? Just as a sighted person sees form by himself but cannot demonstrate it to one born blind, and yet from the mere fact that 'it cannot be demonstrated' it is not understood that 'it does not exist' — so too this person perceives the <s>ātman</s> (self) by himself but cannot show it to another, because the other who would be the observer lacks the capacity to perceive that person [i.e., the self]. That other person too perceives his own self by himself, not the self of another. Therefore, all [persons], each perceiving the self through his own self, certainly exist, even though they are not perceived by other persons. On this point there is a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> text: 'When speech has ceased, what light does this person have? The self is his light, O king, he said.' That it is not perceived by another — on this too there is a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> text: 'He is ungraspable, for he is not grasped.' The purport of this is that he is not grasped by another. — Why? — Because of the statement of his being self-luminous. On this too there is a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> text: 'Here this person becomes self-luminous.'

body.text: kena punar upāyena ayam anyasmai kathyata iti ? - atrāpy upāye brāhmaṇaṃ bhavati śa eṣa neti nety ātmneti hovāca" iti / asāv "ayam evaṃrūpa" iti na śakyate nidarśayitum / yac ca paraḥ paśyati, tatpratiṣedhas tasyopadeśopāyaḥ / śārīraṃ paraḥ paśyati / tenātmā upadiśyate / "śarīraṃ nātmā; asti śarīrād anyaḥ sa cātmā" iti śarīrapratiṣedhena ātmopadiśyate / tathā prāṇādayo nātmāna iti tatpratiṣedhena tebhyo 'nya upadiśyate / tathā parasthāḥ sukhādayaḥ pareṇa liṅgair upalabhyante / te 'pi nātmāna iti tatpratiledhena tebhyo 'nya upadiśyate /
body.translated_text: But by what means is this [self] communicated to another? — On the means for this too there is a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> text: 'He said: this <s>ātman</s> (self) is "not this, not this" (<s>neti neti</s>).' It cannot be demonstrated [positively] as 'this is of such-and-such a form.' And what the other person perceives — the negation of that is the means of teaching the self. The other person perceives the body. Therefore, the <s>ātman</s> is taught by negating the body: 'The body is not the <s>ātman</s>; there is something other than the body, and that is the <s>ātman</s>' — thus by negating the body, the <s>ātman</s> is taught. Similarly, <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath) and the rest are not the <s>ātman</s> — by negating them, something other than them is taught. Likewise, pleasure (<s>sukha</s>) and other [states] residing in another are perceived by another through inferential signs (<s>liṅga</s>). They too are not the <s>ātman</s> — by negating them, something other than them is taught.

body.text: yaḥ svayaṃ paśyati, na tato 'nyaḥ puruṣa ity etad api puruṣapravṛttyā anumīyate, yadā ' sau puruṣaḥ pūrvedyuḥ sāmikṛtānām arthānāṃ pratisamādhāne śeṣānuṣṭhāne ca yatate / ataḥ pravṛttyāvagamyate ṅūnam asāv anityān nityam avagacchati" iti / upamānāc copadiśyate "yādṛśaṃ bhavān svayam ātmānaṃ paśyati, anenopamānenāvagaccha "aham api tādṛśam eva paśyāmi" iti, yathā kaścid ātmīyāṃ vedanāṃ parasmā ācakṣśīta "dahyamānasyeva me bhavati, yātyamānasyeva me bhavati, rudhyamānasyeva me bhavati" iti / ataḥ svayam avagamyamānatvād asti tadvyatiriktaḥ puruṣa iti /
body.translated_text: That the one who perceives [the self] is not other than the person — this too is inferred from the person's activity, when that person strives on the following day for the settlement and completion of matters accomplished on the previous day. From this activity, it is understood: 'Surely, this one knows the permanent amidst the impermanent.' And [the self] is also taught through analogy (<s>upamāna</s>): 'Just as you yourself see the <s>ātman</s>, understand by this analogy: "I too see [mine] in the same way"' — as when someone describes his own sensation to another: 'I feel as though being burned, I feel as though being dragged, I feel as though being obstructed.' Therefore, since it is known by oneself, there exists a person (<s>puruṣa</s>) distinct from those [pleasures etc.].

body.text: yad apy ucyate "vijñānam apāsya tan nidarśyatām" iti, yady upāyam eva niṣedhasi, na śakyam upāyam antareṇa upeyam upetum / ayam evābhyupāyo jñatavyānām arthānāṃ "yo yathā jñāyate, sa tathā" iti / tad yathā: "kaḥ śuklo nāma?" "yatra śuklatvam asti / " "kiṃ śuklatvaṃ nāma?" "yatra śuklaśabdapravṛttiḥ / " "kva tasya pravṛttiḥ?" "yac chuklaśabda uccarite pratīyate / " tasmān na vijñānaṃ pratyākhyāya kasyacid rūpaṃ nidarśayituṃ śakyam /
body.translated_text: As for the objection 'setting aside consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>), demonstrate it' — if you are denying the very means [of demonstration], the goal cannot be reached without the means. This indeed is the approach for things to be known: 'that which is known in a certain way, is thus.' For example: 'What is called white?' 'That in which whiteness exists.' 'What is whiteness?' 'That to which the word "white" applies.' 'Where does it apply?' 'That which is understood when the word "white" is uttered.' Therefore, it is not possible to demonstrate the nature of anything by setting aside consciousness.

body.text: na ca niyogataḥ pratyaye pratīte pratyayārthaḥ pratīto bhavati / apratīte 'pi hi pratyaye saty arthaḥ pratīyata eva / na hi vijñānaṃ pratyakṣaṃ, vijñeyo 'rthaḥ pratyaka ity etat pūrvam evoktam / tad avaśyakartavye 'pahnave kāmaṃ vijñānam apahnūyeta nārtha ity etad apy uktam eva / tasmād asti sukhādibhyo 'nyo nityaḥ puruṣa iti /
body.translated_text: And it is not the case that when a cognition is necessarily perceived, the object of that cognition is [thereby] perceived. For even without the cognition being perceived, the object is indeed perceived. For consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) is not directly perceived (<s>pratyakṣa</s>); it is the object to be known that is directly perceived — this has already been stated before. Therefore, if a denial must be made, let consciousness be denied, not the object — this too has been stated already. Therefore, there exists a permanent <s>puruṣa</s> (person/self) distinct from pleasure (<s>sukha</s>) and the like.

body.text: atha yad uktaṃ "vijñānaghana evaitebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ samutthāya tāny evānuvinaśyati, na pretya saṃjñāsti" iti, atrocyate: "atraiva mā bhagavān mohāntam āpīpadad" iti 1 paricodanottarakāle 'pahnutya mohāntābhiprāyam asya vacanasya varṇitavān ṅa vāre 'haṃ mohaṃ bravīmi, avināśī vāre 'yam ātmā anucchittidharmā, mātrāsaṃsargas tv asya bhavati" iti / tasmān na vijñānamātram / tasmād vai1amyam / yad uktaṃ ṅa caiṣa "yāti" iti vidhiśabda" iti, mā bhūd vidhiśabdaḥ / śvargakāmo yajeta" iti vacanāntareṇa avagatam anuvadiṣyate / tasmād avirodhaḥ /
body.translated_text: Now, as for what was stated—"Having arisen as a mass of consciousness (<s>vijñānaghana</s>) from these elements, it perishes along with them; there is no awareness after death"—to this it is replied [in the Upaniṣad]: "Here indeed, O Blessed One, you have led me to utter bewilderment." At the time of responding to this objection, having retracted, he described the intended meaning of this statement as conducive to confusion: "I do not speak confusion, O dear one. This <s>ātman</s> (self) is imperishable, of the nature of non-destruction; but its association with the sense-elements (<s>mātrā</s>) undergoes [change]." Therefore [the self] is not mere consciousness. Therefore there is a discrepancy [in the opponent's position]. As for what was said—"And this word 'yāti' (goes) is not an injunctive word"—let it not be an injunctive word. What is known through another statement—"One who desires heaven should sacrifice (<s>svargakāmo yajeta</s>)"—is being restated [here]. Therefore there is no contradiction.
